sections.overview: The okapi is a forest-dwelling giraffid native to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its short neck and compact body contrast with the tall giraffe, its closest living relative. Pale bands on the hindquarters and legs do not make it a relative of zebras.
sections.identification: Adults have a sturdy body, sloping back, short neck and upright ears. The torso is dark brown to reddish; cream-white bands cross the rump and upper legs. Males bear two short, skin-covered ossicones; females lack them. Both sexes use a long dark tongue to grasp leaves and ruminate. Adults stand about 1.5 m at the shoulder and weigh roughly 200–350 kg. San Diego Zoo reports females at about 225–350 kg and males at about 200–300 kg; the female is therefore not necessarily lighter. No reliable sex-specific body-length range or body width was found in that source.
sections.habitat: Its known range is northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, including Ituri. It inhabits dense tropical forest. The IUCN assessment records it from about 450 to 1,500 metres elevation. The Okapi Wildlife Reserve protects a major part of Ituri forest.
sections.diet: This browser eats leaves, buds and shoots from shrubs and low branches, as well as fruit and fungi. The Okapi Conservation Project reports leaves from over one hundred plant and tree species in its diet. Foods vary by place and season. Okapis also eat clay or soil, probably for minerals, though its nutritional role is uncertain.
sections.behavior: Okapis are usually solitary; females stay with calves. Adults may use overlapping areas, while males can exclude other males. Foot glands leave scent traces; males also mark with urine. Calls include coughs, bleats and whistles. Very low calls have been linked to mother–calf communication, though their function remains uncertain.
sections.reproduction: Gestation lasts about fourteen to sixteen months; births are usually single. Calves resemble adults and stand soon after birth. A mother may leave a calf hidden while feeding, then return to nurse. Young sample solid food within weeks. Maturity near three years is reported mainly from managed animals.
sections.ecology: Okapis browse forest vegetation and are prey for leopards. Conservation programmes use this distinctive animal as an emblem for protecting the Ituri forest, benefiting other species sharing its habitat.
sections.conservation: The 2015 IUCN assessment classified the okapi as Endangered, estimating a decline over 50% across three generations. This is the assessment date, not a new 2026 measurement. Pressures include poaching, forest loss and degradation, and insecurity. The Ituri reserve and local conservation programs support protection.
